Seminar Title:

Development of sustainable adsorbent for cationic dye removal: A fresh start for waste valorization

Seminar Type:

Department:

Speaker Name:

susant Mohapatra (522cr1003)

Speaker Type:

04 Dec 2025 5:00 PM

Contact:

Prof. Sunipa Bhattacharyya (CR)

Abstract:

Industrial wastewater treatment has been a significant global issue in recent decades, and waste management requires the development of new, cost-effective, and sustainable technologies. There is a significant demand for innovative wastewater purification methods that utilize eco-friendly, low-cost materials. Adsorption is the most affordable, reliable, and quickly operational wastewater treatment method [1]. In the 21st century, the growing demand for environmentally friendly, porous geopolymer adsorbents may be met by producing them from industrial waste through the concept of a circular economy. This work presents a cost-effective, porous, and shaped fly-ash-based adsorbent for efficiently removing cationic dyes from wastewater. Various percentages of GGBS and clay are combined with fly ash to improve the removal efficiency of the synthesized adsorbent. Parent batches are activated using an activator solution of sodium silicate and sodium hydroxide to prepare the geopolymer slurry. To create a foamed slurry with good workability, sodium dodecyl sulfate was added as a foaming agent. Using the injection solidification process, the slurry was injected dropwise into the PEG-600 medium using a syringe. The bead-shaped adsorbents are then cleaned and dried. Standard techniques (FTIR, XRF, XRD, and SEM-EDX) were used to characterize the adsorbents. Methylene blue (MB), a hazardous dye, was removed from water using batch mode to assess the adsorbents' adsorption capabilities. The ideal geopolymer-shaped adsorbent demonstrated a high adsorption efficiency of 97% for a 10 mg/L MB dye solution at room temperature. The adsorption kinetics and isotherm were studied to elucidate the factors influencing the adsorption mechanism and how the geopolymer's unique ion exchange capabilities generally facilitate its adsorption of MB. The study thoroughly examines the adsorbent's features, including the regeneration and desorption processes.
